summary:
SPHEREx Sky Explorer is a free web tool that lets anyone compare sky images taken months apart, spot what moved, and measure how far. NASA’s SPHEREx telescope maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours about every six months, and comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs, or even a distant “Planet X” could be hidden in the changes between maps.

We built a browser app with a pass slider, a blink comparison, automatic highlighting of moving objects, and a 102-band selector. For each object, you click its position in picture 1 and then picture 2. The tool draws the path, reads longitude and latitude, and calculates the distance with the Euclidean formula. A small neural network scores each candidate as a real mover or an artifact. Reports can be downloaded.

It matters because it makes complex NASA data accessible to students and the public, and gives researchers a quick list of candidates to check. Our demo uses synthetic data and uploaded images. Real FITS support is next.
details:
SPHEREx Sky Explorer is a free browser tool that helps anyone find and measure moving objects in sky images taken months apart. NASA’s SPHEREx telescope maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours about every six months, so comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs, or a possible Planet X appear as sources that change position. Our tool subtracts one image from another, pairs each vanished source with the nearest newly appeared one, and highlights it. The user clicks the object in picture 1 and picture 2. The tool draws the path, reads the longitude and latitude, and calculates the distance with the Euclidean formula. A small neural network scores each candidate as a real mover or an artifact, and a report can be downloaded. Extra pages include a 3D Space Lab.

Benefits: it needs no installation, and it is simple enough for students while giving researchers a candidate list to check. Impact: it makes NASA sky data easier to explore and encourages public participation.

Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript with Canvas, a Python helper script (astroquery) for fetching data, and GitHub Pages for hosting. Creative parts: animated 3D sky background, blink-and-glide comparison, and step-by-step distance animation. We considered limits openly: the demo sky is synthetic, there is no WCS support yet, and all detections are candidates, not confirmed discoveries.
